label: Asymptotic Theory of Statistical Inference
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 165 through 177, asks a single geometric question: when data form a small cloud at scale one over root N around the truth, which features of the model decide whether an estimator uses that cloud efficiently. Consistency, Fisher efficiency, and curvature all become geometry here.

label: Asymptotics as Local Geometry
notes: A parametric model is a surface of distributions; an estimator reads a sample and returns a point on it. For large N the observed sufficient statistic fluctuates at order one over root N, so the surface is studied through its tangent space plus a few curvature corrections. Statistical phrases translate directly into coordinates.

label: MLE in a Full Exponential Family
notes: In a full exponential family the sample mean of the sufficient statistic is an expectation-coordinate point. Matching the model expectation to that observed point gives the maximum likelihood estimate, so in eta coordinates the estimator is simply the observed point itself. There is no geometric detour, only the shrinking error cloud.

label: Cramer-Rao Bound and the Fisher Ellipse
notes: The observed expectation point has covariance about the inverse Fisher information divided by N, drawn as an ellipse that shrinks like one over root N. This is the visual form of the Cramer-Rao lower bound: no unbiased estimator can do better than this Fisher ellipse at first order, and equality defines efficiency.

label: Curved Families and Projection
notes: A curved exponential family is a lower-dimensional submanifold inside a flat ambient family. The observed point usually misses the model, so an estimator must choose a return rule. The maximum likelihood rule is the information-geometric projection, dropping the observed point onto the curve along the Fisher-normal direction.

label: Ancillary Fibers Define the Estimator
notes: Fix a model point eta of u; the ambient observations assigned that same estimate form the fiber A of u. Together the fibers foliate a neighborhood, giving local coordinates u along the model and v along the fiber. Consistency forces each fiber to pass through its model point.

label: Fisher Efficiency as Orthogonality
notes: Efficiency adds an angle condition: at first order the ancillary fiber must meet the model orthogonally in the Fisher metric. A tilted fiber leaks normal noise into the reported u and inflates variance. Eliminating the fiber coordinate by a Schur complement gives the first-order precision of u-tilde.

label: Higher-Order Asymptotics and Curvature
notes: First-order theory sees only the tangent. After bias correction, second-order covariance splits into three nonnegative curvature terms: of the model, of the chosen coordinates, and of the ancillary family. The bias-corrected MLE is special because its ancillary family is m-flat, so the estimator-dependent curvature term vanishes.

label: Testing Shares the Same Geometry
notes: A large-sample test draws a rejection boundary that approaches the null point as N grows; varying the null turns these boundaries into another ancillary family. So estimation and testing share first-order geometry. Rao, Wald, and likelihood-ratio tests agree in the tangent approximation but differ at second order through boundary angle and curvature.

label: Recap and Boundary Cases
notes: To summarize: the MLE is a projection, ancillary fibers encode the estimator, consistency needs fibers through the model, efficiency needs orthogonality, and curvature explains second-order differences. The chapter warns that MLE optimality need not persist to every order, and that non-regular models break the Riemannian story entirely.
